case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a nonretroactive statutory amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) may itself qualify as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) for defendants whose sentences were already final.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) (compassionate release / sentence reduction for “extraordinary and compelling reasons”), in interaction with Congress’s amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) in the First Step Act (changing the “stacking” of mandatory minimums while specifying nonretroactivity for already-final sentences).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)’s text and history give sentencing courts broad discretion to identify “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and that the dramatic sentencing disparity created by Congress’s later § 924(c) anti-stacking reform—though expressly nonretroactive—can still be considered an extraordinary and compelling reason for individualized sentence reduction, subject to the district court’s weighing of the § 3553(a) factors.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that allowing a concededly nonretroactive § 924(c) amendment to qualify as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” would effectively make the amendment retroactive in practice, contradicting Congress’s express choice not to apply the amendment to preexisting final sentences; therefore, a court of appeals correctly rejects reliance on the nonretroactive amendment as the necessary “extraordinary and compelling” basis for relief under § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i).
key_precedents: Concepcion v. United States (district court discretion to consider information when Congress authorizes resentencing/reduction)
Dillon v. United States (sentence modification proceedings are limited by statute; not full resentencings)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest textual point: § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express prohibition on considering nonretroactive changes, and Concepcion suggests broad consideration once Congress opens a modification mechanism. But that argument elides the antecedent eligibility question—whether the nonretroactive § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment itself can supply the “extraordinary and compelling” reason—where Dillon’s framing of § 3582(c) as a narrow exception to finality is the closer fit and counsels reading the open-textured threshold in harmony with Congress’s specific prospective-only judgment. I can accept a narrow middle ground: sentencing disparity from the amendment may be considered as context once some independent, defendant-specific extraordinary circumstance is shown, but the conceded nonretroactive change cannot do the threshold work standing alone without effectively recreating the retroactivity Congress withheld. Concepcion does not undermine that line because, as Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch note, it addresses what may be considered after eligibility is established, not what may establish eligibility in the first place.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest textual point: § 3582(c)(1)(A) does not expressly forbid considering nonretroactive legal changes, and the provision functions as an individualized safety valve. But on an originalist, structural reading, the open-ended phrase “extraordinary and compelling” must be construed in harmony with Congress’s specific prospective-only judgment about § 924(c) anti-stacking; otherwise courts would use that general language to accomplish, case by case, the retroactivity Congress deliberately withheld. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, Concepcion addresses the permissible scope of consideration once a resentencing mechanism applies; it does not answer the antecedent eligibility question whether a nonretroactive amendment may itself supply the threshold “extraordinary and compelling” reason, and Dillon remains the closer guide that § 3582(c) is a narrow, statutorily bounded exception to finality. I therefore would allow the disparity only as context once some independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, but not as the qualifying reason standing alone.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best textual point: § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) contains no express prohibition on considering nonretroactive changes, and Concepcion reflects a general presumption of broad informational scope once Congress opens a modification mechanism. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, that answers the downstream “what may be considered” question, not the antecedent eligibility question—whether the very nonretroactive § 924(c) anti-stacking change can itself supply the “extraordinary and compelling” reason without effectively reintroducing the retroactivity Congress withheld. Dillon remains the closer structural guide: § 3582(c) is a tightly cabined exception to finality, and reading “extraordinary and compelling” to include, standing alone, the precise prospective-only change Congress chose not to make retroactive would collapse that line in operation. I’m still open to disparity playing a contextual role once independent, individualized extraordinary circumstances are shown, but I do not think the amendment itself can do the threshold work.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is the finality/nonretroactivity concern: reading the § 924(c) anti-stacking disparity as “extraordinary and compelling” could approximate retroactivity Congress withheld. But that argument assumes an atextual eligibility carveout—Congress chose prospective-only application to block automatic reopening, yet it simultaneously preserved (and broadened access to) an individualized safety valve that requires a demanding “extraordinary and compelling” finding plus § 3553(a) screening, which prevents the categorical, across-the-board effect Roberts and Justice Thomas fear. Dillon’s “narrow exception” framing supports enforcing the statutory constraints Congress wrote, not adding a prohibition Congress did not; and as Justice Kagan notes, Concepcion reinforces the default presumption that courts may consider intervening legal developments absent a clear textual bar, which I do not see here. I would accept a limiting principle—disparity is not dispositive and must be assessed case-by-case—but I cannot endorse a rule that forbids considering the extreme stacking disparity at the threshold when it may be precisely what makes a case extraordinary.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is the Dillon/finality concern—that reading the nonretroactive § 924(c) change itself as “extraordinary and compelling” risks case-by-case retroactivity Congress declined. But under a pragmatic textualism, the harmony Dillon demands is with the criteria Congress actually enacted in § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i): an open-textured, individualized “extraordinary and compelling” inquiry plus § 3553(a), not an atextual categorical exclusion of disparities caused by nonretroactivity. Concepcion doesn’t decide the eligibility question, but it supports the baseline interpretive presumption that courts may consider intervening legal changes absent an express statutory bar; here, Congress chose prospectivity for automatic reopening, yet left compassionate release as a separate safety valve without carving out this category. I can accept Roberts’s limiting principle as a narrowing construction—disparity alone will rarely suffice and cannot be treated as dispositive—but I would not read the statute to forbid considering that disparity at the threshold when it contributes to an “extraordinary and compelling” showing in context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s textual point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) contains no express bar on considering nonretroactive legal changes—has force, but it does not answer how to read “extraordinary and compelling” in a statute that is, as Dillon stresses, a narrow exception to finality. Harmonizing statutes, Congress’s deliberate choice to make the § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment prospective-only is a specific judgment that courts should not effectively undo by treating that very nonretroactivity-driven disparity as the threshold “extraordinary and compelling” reason. Concepcion, as the Chief Justice explains, is about the scope of considerations once Congress has opened a resentencing channel for a defined class; it does not license expanding eligibility under § 3582(c) to encompass a conceded nonretroactive change as such. I would leave room to consider the disparity as context once some independent, individualized extraordinary circumstance is shown, but the statutory change alone cannot do the eligibility work without intruding on Congress’s retroactivity line.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point remains textual: § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express exclusion for nonretroactive legal changes, and Concepcion reflects a general presumption of broad consideration once Congress authorizes a modification proceeding. But Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is more persuasive under § 3582(c)’s structure and Dillon: compassionate release is a narrow exception to finality with a threshold eligibility requirement that should be construed in harmony with Congress’s specific prospective-only judgment about § 924(c) anti-stacking, lest courts effectively supply judge-by-judge retroactivity for the very change Congress declined to make retroactive. Concepcion is distinguishable because it speaks primarily to what may be considered after an authorized resentencing mechanism applies, not to whether a nonretroactive statutory change can itself satisfy the antecedent “extraordinary and compelling” trigger. I would allow the disparity to be considered as contextual once some independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, but not to do the threshold work standing alone.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest textual point: § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) contains no express bar on considering nonretroactive legal changes, and Concepcion reflects a general permissiveness about what a court may consider in a sentence-modification proceeding. But I agree with the Chief Justice’s framing that the antecedent issue is what may supply eligibility—Dillon is closer because it treats § 3582(c) as a narrow, statutorily bounded exception to finality, so “extraordinary and compelling” should not be read to allow a concededly prospective-only § 924(c) amendment to do the threshold work on its own. Reading the anti-stacking disparity as sufficient, standing alone, would in practice produce judge-by-judge retroactivity for the very reform Congress affirmatively withheld from prior sentences, undermining the original public meaning of the statute’s finality-preserving structure. Concepcion remains distinguishable because it addresses the breadth of consideration after Congress has opened a resentencing mechanism for a defined class, not whether a nonretroactive legal change can itself trigger the compassionate-release eligibility threshold.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s finality/nonretroactivity point seriously: if the § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment alone always satisfied “extraordinary and compelling,” courts could approximate retroactivity that Congress declined to provide. But that concern does not justify adding an atextual categorical exclusion at the eligibility stage; Congress already chose an individualized safety valve requiring a demanding threshold finding plus a separate § 3553(a) assessment, which preserves finality through discretion rather than automatic reopening. Concepcion, as Justice Kagan stresses, reinforces the baseline that when Congress authorizes a sentence-modification mechanism and does not expressly bar considering intervening law, courts may weigh it—so long as they do not treat it as dispositive or automatic. Dillon’s “narrow exception” framing (invoked by Roberts/Thomas) cuts against freewheeling resentencing, but it does not compel reading “extraordinary and compelling” to exclude precisely the kind of extreme sentencing disparity Congress itself identified as unjust, especially when considered in combination with individualized circumstances.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3582(c) is a narrow exception to the rule that a final sentence “may not [be] modify[ied]” absent statutory authorization, and Dillon v. United States instructs that such sentence-modification proceedings are limited by the scope Congress set. Here Congress amended § 924(c) to curb “stacking” but expressly chose nonretroactivity for already-final sentences; treating that very nonretroactivity-driven disparity as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” under § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) risks functionally overriding Congress’s retroactivity line and undermining institutional legitimacy. Concepcion recognizes broad discretion when Congress authorizes resentencing, but it does not permit courts to use § 3582(c)(1)(A) to accomplish retroactivity Congress withheld. A court may still consider individualized, defendant-specific circumstances as “extraordinary and compelling,” but the nonretroactive change in § 924(c) cannot itself do that work.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of § 3582(c)(1)(A) make sentence modification an exception to finality that exists only within the limits Congress prescribed, and courts may not use the open-ended phrase “extraordinary and compelling reasons” to achieve retroactivity Congress expressly withheld for the First Step Act’s § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment. Reading a concededly nonretroactive change in § 924(c) to be, by itself, an “extraordinary and compelling” reason effectively nullifies Congress’s nonretroactivity choice and expands judicial power beyond the statute’s original public meaning. Dillon v. United States confirms that § 3582(c) proceedings are not plenary resentencings and are constrained by the governing statute, which here does not authorize courts to treat a nonretroactive amendment as a backdoor resentencing mandate. Concepcion does not compel a different result because it addressed what courts may consider once Congress has authorized a particular resentencing mechanism, not whether § 3582(c)(1)(A) can be used to override Congress’s explicit decision to deny categorical retroactive effect.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow, statute-bound exception to the rule of finality, and it authorizes reductions only when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant relief; it does not create a roving power to implement nonretroactive legislative changes case by case. Congress expressly amended § 924(c) to curb “stacking” while specifying that the change would not apply to defendants with already-final sentences, and treating that nonretroactive amendment itself as an “extraordinary and compelling” reason would effectively override Congress’s retroactivity choice in practice. Dillon v. United States confirms that § 3582(c) proceedings are limited and must respect the constraints Congress enacted, rather than operating as de facto resentencings. Concepcion’s recognition of discretion when Congress authorizes resentencing does not answer the threshold question here—whether the nonretroactive amendment can qualify as the required “extraordinary and compelling” reason in the first place.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a court to reduce a final sentence upon finding “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and Congress did not expressly bar courts from considering later legal changes—so a dramatic § 924(c) anti-stacking disparity may qualify as such a reason in an individualized case. Concepcion v. United States confirms the “long and durable tradition” of broad sentencing discretion to consider intervening legal developments (even if nonretroactive) when Congress has opened a sentence-modification door, and nothing in § 3582(c)(1)(A) or the First Step Act’s nonretroactivity clause for § 924(c) forecloses consideration of the disparity as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling inquiry. Dillon v. United States shows these proceedings are statutorily bounded, but here the statute’s bound is the requirement of “extraordinary and compelling reasons” plus the § 3553(a) factors—not a categorical prohibition on considering nonretroactive reforms. Allowing courts to weigh the § 924(c) change as one factor respects Congress’s choice not to grant automatic retroactivity while preserving compassionate release’s equitable function for disproportionately harsh sentences, especially affecting vulnerable defendants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a sentence reduction when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” exist, and nothing in its text (or in § 994(t)’s limited carveout) forbids a court from considering a later, nonretroactive change in sentencing law as part of that assessment, so long as the court still applies the § 3553(a) factors. Congress’s decision to make the § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment nonretroactive means courts may not automatically reopen all final sentences, but it does not clearly withdraw the separate, case-by-case “safety valve” Congress preserved in § 3582(c)(1)(A). Concepcion supports reading sentence-modification statutes to permit consideration of intervening legal changes absent an express textual prohibition, while Dillon confirms the proceeding remains constrained by the statute—here, individualized determinations under “extraordinary and compelling” plus § 3553(a), not a wholesale retroactive resentencing regime. Allowing courts to treat the resulting sentencing disparity as potentially extraordinary and compelling, without making it dispositive, best harmonizes § 3582(c)(1)(A) with Congress’s nonretroactivity choice and preserves a workable middle ground.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) creates a narrow exception to the rule of finality, permitting a reduction only when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” warrant it, and Congress expressly chose in the First Step Act not to make its § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment retroactive to already-final sentences. Treating that nonretroactive change itself as the qualifying “extraordinary and compelling” reason would functionally override Congress’s nonretroactivity line and upset separation-of-powers principles by allowing courts to accomplish through compassionate release what Congress withheld by statute. Dillon confirms that § 3582(c) proceedings are “limited by statute” and not full resentencings; whatever discretion Concepcion recognizes when Congress authorizes a resentencing-like reduction does not permit courts to rewrite the threshold eligibility standard in § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) to incorporate nonretroactive statutory amendments as such. Absent clearer textual direction from Congress (or a Sentencing Commission policy statement under § 994(t) addressing this category), the better reading is that the nonretroactive § 924(c) amendment cannot itself supply the required extraordinary-and-compelling basis.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A) is a narrow, statutory exception to the rule of finality, and under Dillon v. United States sentence-modification proceedings are limited by the constraints Congress and the Sentencing Commission have imposed, not treated as freewheeling resentencings. Congress in the First Step Act expressly chose not to make the § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment retroactive to already-final sentences, and allowing that nonretroactive change to itself qualify as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” would largely circumvent that legislative choice in practice. Nothing in the First Step Act clearly displaces Congress’s separate delegation in 28 U.S.C. § 994(t) to the Commission to define “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” including Congress’s demonstrated willingness to specify limits (e.g., rehabilitation alone may not suffice). Concepcion recognizes district-court discretion when Congress authorizes resentencing, but it does not authorize courts to use § 3582(c)(1)(A) to effectuate retroactivity Congress withheld.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a narrow exception to finality only when a court finds “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and that phrase cannot be read to treat Congress’s expressly nonretroactive amendment to § 924(c) as the reason itself without effectively overriding Congress’s nonretroactivity choice in the First Step Act. Dillon v. United States emphasizes that sentence-modification proceedings are constrained by the statute’s limits, and here the relevant limit is that Congress amended § 924(c) prospectively only, reserving retroactivity decisions to itself. Concepcion v. United States is distinguishable because it concerned the scope of what a court may consider once Congress has affirmatively authorized a resentencing for a class of defendants; it does not compel the conclusion that a court may use § 3582(c)(1)(A) to achieve retroactivity Congress withheld. A court may still consider individualized circumstances under § 3553(a), but the nonretroactive change to § 924(c) cannot, standing alone, qualify as an “extraordinary and compelling” reason under § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a sentence reduction when a court finds “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and nothing in its text (or in § 994(t)) excludes consideration of a later-enacted, nonretroactive statutory change as part of that individualized assessment. Congress’s choice to make the First Step Act’s § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment nonretroactive bars automatic resentencing for all past cases, but it does not clearly forbid courts from treating the resulting sentencing disparity as one factor that may qualify as “extraordinary and compelling,” subject to the required § 3553(a) analysis. Concepcion supports that when Congress opens a sentence-reduction doorway, district courts may consider intervening changes in law or fact—including nonretroactive ones—absent an express statutory prohibition, and that approach respects both procedural fairness and practical consequences in extreme cases. Dillon confirms these proceedings are constrained by statute, but here the statute’s broad “extraordinary and compelling” standard—followed by § 3553(a) balancing—provides the limiting principle without reading into Congress’s nonretroactivity choice an additional, unwritten categorical bar.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court may treat Congress’s non-retroactive amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)’s sentencing scheme as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” to reduce a final sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) (compassionate release / sentence-reduction authority requiring “extraordinary and compelling reasons”), with the asserted “reason” being Congress’s amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) that Congress specified would not apply to already-final sentences (non-retroactivity clause in the amending legislation).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s text and history confer broad equitable discretion on sentencing courts to identify “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and that dramatic sentencing disparities created by Congress’s later amendment to § 924(c)—even if expressly non-retroactive—can still qualify as extraordinary and compelling in an individual case; they emphasize fairness, individualized review, and that compassionate release does not “make the amendment retroactive” categorically but permits case-by-case relief.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that allowing non-retroactive § 924(c) amendments to count as “extraordinary and compelling reasons” would effectively circumvent Congress’s express decision not to reopen final sentences, converting § 3582(c)(1)(A) into a vehicle for de facto retroactivity; because Congress specified the amendment does not apply to preexisting sentences, that change cannot itself supply the extraordinary-and-compelling predicate required for a reduction.
key_precedents: Not specified in the provided excerpts (the documents quoted identify the question presented and procedural posture but do not quote or list Supreme Court precedents).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest textual point: Congress expressly barred “rehabilitation alone” in § 994(t) and did not similarly bar consideration of non-retroactive legal changes under § 3582(c)(1)(A). But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize, Concepcion addresses the scope of information a court may consider once a sentence-modification proceeding is properly authorized; it does not answer whether a concededly non-retroactive amendment can itself satisfy the threshold “extraordinary and compelling” gateway, and Dillon’s finality-centered framework counsels against reading that gateway to undo Congress’s explicit nonretroactivity line-drawing. Under a minimalist, harmonizing approach, the § 924(c) stacking change can be weighed at the § 3553(a) stage after some independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, but it cannot be the sole predicate without turning compassionate release into discretionary retroactivity. Justice Sotomayor’s institutional concern cuts both ways, but I think our narrow rule better preserves legitimacy by respecting Congress’s temporal choice while leaving room for individualized mercy where the statute already permits it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest textual point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) contains no express exclusion for non-retroactive legal changes, unlike § 994(t)’s rehabilitation-alone rule—does not answer the distinct question whether Congress’s express nonretroactivity judgment in the § 924(c) amendment may itself supply the threshold “extraordinary and compelling” predicate. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Concepcion concerns the range of considerations once a defendant is already eligible for a modification proceeding; it does not convert a concededly non-retroactive change into the statutory gateway that opens the proceeding. Reading the stacking change as the gateway would, in operation, nullify Congress’s temporal line by authorizing judge-by-judge retroactivity, which a textualist should avoid when harmonizing related enactments and respecting § 3582(c) as a narrow exception to finality described in Dillon. The better rule remains that the disparity may be weighed under § 3553(a) after some independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, preserving discretion without overriding Congress’s nonretroactivity choice.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is broadly phrased and that Congress knows how to write categorical exclusions (as in § 994(t))—cannot carry the day because it treats silence as authorization to undo Congress’s explicit temporal line-drawing elsewhere. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh correctly emphasize that Concepcion addresses what information a court may consider once a sentence-modification proceeding is properly authorized; it does not resolve the threshold question whether a concededly non-retroactive statutory change can itself supply the “extraordinary and compelling” predicate. Dillon reinforces that § 3582(c) is a narrow, statute-bound exception to finality, so using the non-retroactive § 924(c) stacking fix as the gateway effectively repackages nonretroactivity into discretionary, judge-by-judge retroactivity. The stacking change may still be relevant at the § 3553(a) stage after an independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, preserving individualized discretion without converting compassionate release into a general retroactivity valve.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is finality and the risk of case-by-case “shadow retroactivity,” anchored in Dillon’s description of § 3582(c) as a narrow statutory exception. But that concern cannot justify reading an atextual categorical bar into § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i), especially when (as Justice Kagan notes) Congress showed in § 994(t) it knows how to impose explicit exclusions and chose not to do so for non-retroactive legal changes. Concepcion does not answer the threshold question by itself, but it reinforces the interpretive baseline that, absent an express statutory prohibition, district courts may consider intervening legal developments as part of an individualized, discretionary inquiry—filtered through § 3553(a)—without deeming the amendment automatically retroactive. Under my pragmatic approach, the respondents’ proposed “independent extraordinary circumstance” gatekeeping rule is overinclusive and would blind courts to rare, extreme stacking disparities that now stand out as unjust and that compassionate release was designed to address.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the circumvention/finality concern: letting the nonretroactive § 924(c) change itself qualify as “extraordinary and compelling” could look like case-by-case retroactivity. But that argument still depends on adding a categorical threshold exclusion Congress did not write into § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i), and the text/structure cut the other way—Congress showed in § 994(t) it knows how to bar specific considerations (rehabilitation alone) and it did not similarly bar nonretroactive legal changes, leaving courts to apply the statute’s built-in backstops (individualized findings plus § 3553(a)). Dillon reinforces that § 3582(c) is constrained, but the constraint is that courts may reduce only when a reason is “extraordinary and compelling” and the § 3553(a) factors warrant it; recognizing a dramatic stacking disparity as potentially extraordinary does not “apply” the amendment retroactively, it uses compassionate release as the narrow safety valve Congress preserved. Concepcion, as Justice Roberts notes, is not an eligibility case, but it supports the interpretive baseline that we should not invent extra eligibility bars absent clear text—especially where Congress expressly addressed nonretroactivity in the § 924(c) amendment without purporting to narrow compassionate release.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is textual: Congress expressly barred “rehabilitation alone” in § 994(t) yet did not similarly exclude non-retroactive legal changes from § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i), and Concepcion reflects broad discretion absent express limits. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Concepcion presupposes an authorized modification proceeding and does not resolve the antecedent gateway question; reading an expressly non-retroactive § 924(c) amendment itself as the “extraordinary and compelling” reason would, in operation, reintroduce retroactivity through judicial discretion and thereby negate Congress’s temporal line. Dillon’s understanding of § 3582(c) as a narrow, statute-bound exception to finality reinforces that courts may weigh the stacking disparity under § 3553(a) once some independent extraordinary circumstance exists, but may not use Congress’s nonretroactive change as the sole trigger for eligibility. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about adding atextual categorical bars is real, yet under a textualist/originalist methodology the better harmony is to respect Congress’s explicit nonretroactivity decision while preserving individualized discretion within the proceeding once properly opened.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan have the strongest textual point: Congress expressly excluded “rehabilitation alone” in § 994(t) and did not similarly exclude non-retroactive legal changes from § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i). But under Dillon’s framework—emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts—§ 3582(c) is a narrow, statute-bound exception to finality, and I cannot read § 3582(c)(1)(A) to let courts treat Congress’s explicit non-retroactivity decision for the § 924(c) stacking fix as itself the “extraordinary and compelling” gateway without functionally recreating retroactivity judge-by-judge. Concepcion, as Roberts and Justice Gorsuch note, addresses the scope of considerations once eligibility exists, not the antecedent threshold question. The harmonizing, institutional rule remains: the § 924(c) change can be weighed at the § 3553(a) stage after some independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, preserving discretion without undermining Congress’s temporal line-drawing and stable final judgments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest textual point: Congress wrote an express exclusion in § 994(t) (rehabilitation alone) but did not similarly bar consideration of non-retroactive legal changes, and Concepcion reflects broad discretion absent express limits. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Concepcion presupposes that a modification proceeding is authorized; it speaks to the scope of what a court may consider once inside the proceeding, not whether the non-retroactive § 924(c) change can itself satisfy § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i)’s threshold “extraordinary and compelling” gateway. Treating Congress’s explicit non-retroactivity line as the very “extraordinary and compelling” reason would functionally negate that line through individualized judicial retroactivity, contrary to Dillon’s understanding of § 3582(c) as a narrow, statute-bound exception to finality. On a textualist, harmonizing reading, the § 924(c) disparity may be weighed under § 3553(a) after an independent extraordinary circumstance is shown, but it cannot alone open the gate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s institutional/finality concern is the strongest point for the Respondent, but it still depends on adding a categorical threshold exclusion that Congress did not write into § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i). Dillon’s “constrained exception to finality” framework is satisfied by the statute’s own constraints—discretionary relief, the § 3553(a) screen, and any applicable policy statement—so recognizing that an extreme § 924(c) stacking disparity can be “extraordinary and compelling” in an individualized case does not itself “apply” the amendment retroactively. Concepcion, as Justice Thomas notes, is not an eligibility case, yet it reinforces the baseline interpretive premise that courts may consider intervening developments absent an express statutory bar; here, Congress included an express limitation elsewhere (§ 994(t)’s rehabilitation-alone rule) but did not similarly bar consideration of nonretroactive legal changes. Under a pragmatic, procedurally fair approach, the Respondent’s proposed gatekeeping rule is overbroad and unnecessary because the existing statutory backstops already prevent routine nonretroactivity complaints from becoming an end-run around Congress.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow, statute-bound exception to the rule of finality, and courts must operate within the limits Congress set when authorizing sentence modifications. See Dillon v. United States (2010) (treating § 3582(c) proceedings as constrained by statute and not a plenary resentencing). Allowing a concededly non-retroactive amendment to § 924(c) to qualify, by itself, as an “extraordinary and compelling reason” would effectively circumvent Congress’s express non-retroactivity choice and invite broad relitigation of final sentences, contrary to § 3582(c)’s limited design and institutional interests in finality. A narrow reading preserves Congress’s retroactivity line-drawing while leaving compassionate release available for genuinely individualized circumstances consistent with the statute’s text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow exception to the rule of finality, permitting a reduction only when the court finds “extraordinary and compelling reasons” consistent with the statute’s constraints; it does not authorize a plenary, equitable resentencing to correct disparities Congress chose not to remedy retroactively. Congress expressly made its § 924(c) amendment non-retroactive, and treating that very non-retroactive change as the predicate “extraordinary and compelling” reason would effectively nullify Congress’s textual choice and convert compassionate release into a de facto retroactivity mechanism. Under a textualist reading that harmonizes related provisions, courts must respect Congress’s non-retroactivity decision rather than use § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) to circumvent it. Dillon v. United States confirms that § 3582(c) proceedings are limited by the statute’s text and are not full resentencings driven by general equitable considerations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow exception to the rule of finality, authorizing reductions only when a defendant shows “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and it should not be read to permit courts to override Congress’s explicit non-retroactivity judgment for the § 924(c) amendment. Treating a deliberately non-retroactive statutory change as the qualifying “reason” would function as de facto retroactivity and would circumvent the separation-of-powers choice Congress made about which sentences to reopen. Dillon v. United States teaches that § 3582(c) proceedings are limited sentence-modification mechanisms, not plenary resentencings, and courts must adhere closely to the statutory constraints Congress imposed. Concepcion does not expand eligibility under § 3582(c)(1)(A) and in fact distinguished compassionate release as permitting reductions only “in certain circumstances,” confirming that eligibility limits matter here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a district court to reduce a sentence for “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and Congress did not textually exclude consideration of non-retroactive legal changes—unlike § 994(t), where Congress expressly limited one category (rehabilitation alone). Under Concepcion v. United States, 597 U.S. 481 (2022), sentencing-modification courts retain broad discretion to consider intervening changes in law and fact unless Congress clearly cabins that discretion, and the § 924(c) non-retroactivity clause does not purport to amend or restrict § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s equitable safety valve. Treating the resulting sentencing disparity as one possible “extraordinary and compelling” reason does not make the amendment categorically retroactive; it permits individualized relief subject to the § 3553(a) factors and the statute’s case-by-case limits. Given the severe real-world consequences of stacked § 924(c) sentences, especially on vulnerable defendants, fairness and access to justice favor allowing courts to consider the disparity as part of the compassionate-release inquiry.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) authorizes a district court to reduce a final sentence when it finds “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and the statute does not textually exclude changes in sentencing law—retroactive or not—from the set of reasons a court may consider. Under Concepcion v. United States, 597 U.S. 481 (2022), sentencing-modification discretion is “bounded only when Congress … expressly limits” what a court may consider, and there is no express limitation in § 3582(c)(1)(A) forbidding consideration of non-retroactive amendments as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling inquiry. Respecting Congress’s non-retroactivity choice for § 924(c) does not require a categorical bar here: compassionate release remains case-specific and still must satisfy § 3582(c)(1)(A)’s requirements, including consistency with applicable policy statements and the § 3553(a) factors, rather than mechanically applying the amendment to all final sentences. A categorical prohibition would read into § 3582(c)(1)(A) a limit Congress did not write and would undermine the provision’s pragmatic function as a safety valve for unusually severe sentences in individual cases.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow exception to the rule of finality, authorizing sentence reductions only when "extraordinary and compelling reasons" exist and otherwise leaving sentencing choices to Congress. In the First Step Act, Congress amended § 924(c)’s stacking rule but expressly made that change non-retroactive; treating that very non-retroactive amendment as the “extraordinary and compelling” reason would effectively accomplish retroactivity through judicial discretion, undermining Congress’s policy choice and separation of powers. Dillon v. United States, 560 U.S. 817 (2010), confirms § 3582(c) proceedings are congressionally cabined sentence-modification mechanisms, not plenary resentencings where courts may revisit sentencing policy wholesale. Whatever room remains for individualized assessment, it cannot be used to nullify a clear non-retroactivity clause by re-labeling it as an “extraordinary and compelling” predicate under § 3582(c)(1)(A)(i).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow exception to the rule of finality, and its “extraordinary and compelling reasons” requirement should not be read to authorize district courts to override Congress’s express non-retroactivity choice for the § 924(c) amendment. Allowing a concededly non-retroactive statutory change to supply the predicate “extraordinary and compelling” reason would, in practical effect, create de facto retroactivity through case-by-case resentencing, undermining Congress’s specific temporal line and the institutional interest in stable, workable sentencing rules. Dillon v. United States confirms that § 3582(c) proceedings are limited sentence-modification mechanisms that must operate within the bounds Congress set, including respect for finality and the Commission’s constrained role in such proceedings. The better reading, consistent with judicial restraint and history of limited post-judgment sentencing modifications, is that the § 924(c) change may inform the § 3553(a) analysis once an independent extraordinary reason is shown, but cannot itself be the extraordinary-and-compelling trigger when Congress made it non-retroactive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) is a narrow exception to the rule of finality, authorizing a sentence reduction only when “extraordinary and compelling reasons” are present and only “consistent with applicable policy statements,” not as a general license to implement later policy preferences. Treating Congress’s expressly non-retroactive amendment to § 924(c) as itself “extraordinary and compelling” would effectively accomplish retroactivity case-by-case, in tension with Congress’s textual choice to withhold retroactive effect in the amending legislation. Dillon v. United States underscores that § 3582(c) proceedings are limited sentence-modification mechanisms bounded by the authority Congress granted, not plenary resentencings that can be used to capture non-retroactive changes. Whatever equitable appeal the disparity has, the better reading is that courts may consider such changes only if some other extraordinary-and-compelling predicate exists, not as the predicate itself.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 3582(c)(1)(A)(i) broadly authorizes a court to reduce a sentence when it finds “extraordinary and compelling reasons,” and nothing in that text categorically excludes Congress’s later non-retroactive § 924(c) amendment from informing that individualized judgment. As Concepcion v. United States, 597 U.S. 481 (2022), explains in the closely related sentence-modification context, district courts retain traditional discretion to consider intervening legal changes (even nonretroactive ones) absent an express statutory prohibition; Congress knows how to impose such limits and did not do so in § 3582(c)(1)(A). Treating the resulting sentencing disparity as a possible “reason” does not “make the amendment retroactive” across the board—it allows case-by-case relief subject to the separate statutory backstops of § 3553(a) and consistency with applicable policy statements under § 3582(c)(1)(A). Given the First Step Act’s emphasis on procedural fairness and individualized review, the better reading preserves district court discretion to consider the nonretroactive § 924(c) change among the totality of circumstances.
